795.bp: As AI systems become smart enough to act without constant human oversight—making decisions about money, scheduling, security—we need a way to know that an agent we're about to trust is real, who built it, and what rules it follows. Right now there's no equivalent to the internet's DNS or certificate authorities for agents, so the web is ripe for impersonation, unaccountable systems, and chaos when autonomous agents from different organizations try to work together.
795.wh: The basic problem is that trust infrastructure—naming, certification, discovery—was designed for static servers, not for mobile, self-updating AI systems that live across clouds, devices, and edge computers and can spawn new agents dynamically. You can't just slap DNS on top of something this fluid. Real governance also means policy compliance (can this agent access sensitive data?) and safe composition (will combining this agent with that one violate my security rules?), which requires machinery for auditing, attestation, and revocation at scale.
795.ap: NANDA borrows the internet's own trust playbook—a root of trust (like ICANN), a naming system (like DNS), certificate authorities that vouch for identity, and delegated authority so you can hand off verification responsibility to others you trust. Instead of protocols for agents talking to each other, it builds the control plane: mechanisms to register agents (so they're discoverable), attest to their properties (proving they haven't been tampered with), and enforce policies across organizational boundaries.
795.ww: The reason this works is that it separates the hard problem (deciding if an agent is trustworthy) from the scaling problem (finding agents and composing them). A clear namespace and public registry let strangers discover agents safely; attestation lets you know an agent hasn't been modified since it was certified; delegated authority lets your organization set its own policies without breaking interoperability. This is exactly what made the web work: you didn't need to trust every server, only the root and the certificate authorities.
795.po: The concrete payoff is a web where autonomous agents can be discovered, verified, and safely combined across organizations. An agent certifies that it follows your data policies; another agent can check that before interacting. No more black-box agents from unknown sources. At scale, this enables the ''agentic web'' where intelligence is distributed but trust isn't—you have a machine-checkable proof of what each agent will and won't do.

796.bp: Tor users believe they're anonymous because their traffic is encrypted, but a determined observer watching the patterns of when data flows and how much arrives can often infer which websites someone visits—without ever seeing the actual web requests. This matters because it defeats a core promise of Tor, and it shows that encryption alone doesn't guarantee privacy.
796.wh: The tricky part is that real Tor traffic is messy. It has irregular bursts (data arrives in unpredictable chunks), variable lengths (some site visits send more data than others), and patterns change over time due to network noise. Earlier systems trained on clean, synthetic data, but they fail when you feed them real Tor exit traffic because the patterns don't match what they learned. Traditional machine learning assumes you have lots of clean examples; here you have a few thousand real examples drowned in noise.
796.ap: RoFiRe uses a combination of two tricks. First, it uses dynamic augmentation—artificially creating variations of training data by warping the patterns in ways that match real Tor noise (irregular bursts, variable lengths). Second, it applies RMS-based pre-normalization, which is a way of scaling down the data so that loud, misleading patterns (like occasional large bursts) don't dominate the learning process. Together, these make the model robust to the messy reality of real traffic.
796.ww: The reason this works is two-fold. Augmentation makes the model practice on data that looks more like real Tor traffic, so it doesn't get surprised when it sees the real thing. Normalization tones down outliers so the model focuses on the fundamental patterns—the fingerprint—rather than getting distracted by random noise. This is like teaching someone to recognize a friend's face in dim light, crowded places, and bad angles, not just in a perfect studio photo.
796.po: The result is a model that correctly identifies visited websites from real Tor traffic 9% more often than prior methods, even on traffic the model has never seen before. This is the first time anyone has convincingly shown that website fingerprinting works on real Tor data, not just synthetic tests. It demonstrates that Tor's anonymity is weaker than users assume—a real privacy risk that motivates better defenses.

797.bp: Real-world systems generate data that changes over time—network traffic, power demand, stock prices—and predicting the next day or month is valuable for planning infrastructure, budgeting, and risk management. The challenge is that these systems have patterns that repeat at different timescales: minute-by-minute fluctuations, daily cycles, seasonal swings, all happening at once.
797.wh: Most forecasting models handle one timescale at a time or average them crudely, losing detail. When you try to mix multiple timescales, you hit two walls: redundancy (the same information appears at different scales, so you're computing it twice) and semantic gaps (the abstract monthly trend and the hourly noise are so different that learning from both at once is hard). Real data is also noisy, which makes learning inefficient unless you have tricks to focus the model on signal rather than noise.
797.ap: SEMixer stacks two ideas. The Random Attention Mechanism picks different subsets of the data during training (like dropout), so the model learns multiple ways to predict the same thing; at prediction time, it averages these diverse views. The Multiscale Progressive Mixing Chain then chains together these mechanisms in a way that lets information flow from fine-grained patterns to coarse ones progressively. The key insight is that once you've extracted the fine grain, the coarser scales are just combinations of what you already have.
797.ww: This works because diversity in training (via random selection) forces the model to learn robust patterns rather than memorizing noise. By mixing progressively—fine to coarse—you avoid redundancy: the coarse mixer only needs to combine fine patterns it's already seen. And because you're using simple math operations (mixing, not deep neural networks), the model stays lightweight and efficient, even with lots of data.
797.po: SEMixer beats ten public benchmarks at long-term forecasting and even placed third in a real-world competition on 21GB of wireless network data. It's both efficient (trains fast, runs light) and accurate, suggesting that the right architectural choice for mixing timescales can outweigh adding more parameters or depth.

798.bp: Scientific knowledge graphs—databases that capture what research says by encoding papers as structured facts—are powerful tools for AI systems that generate answers (they let you ground generated answers in real papers rather than hallucinating). But these databases are built by many contributors, and the quality suffers from inconsistency: duplicate properties with different names, vague definitions, overlapping meanings.
798.wh: The core problem is that crowdsourcing is uncontrolled. When dozens of people independently create properties (kinds of relationships between papers and their contents) without coordination, you get synonyms (multiple names for the same concept), redundancy (overlapping definitions), and ambiguity (unclear semantics). An AI system trying to use these properties for reasoning gets confused when it encounters ten property names meaning essentially the same thing.
798.ap: The paper introduces a semi-automated workflow: large language models scan the entire property set and propose which properties are duplicates or synonyms, which naming conventions are inconsistent, and how to consolidate them. Human experts then review these suggestions and make final decisions, creating a cleaned, unified ontology. The LLM does the heavy lifting of identifying patterns; humans apply judgment and maintain control.
798.ww: This works because LLMs are good at semantic similarity—spotting that 'publication_venue' and 'published_at_conference' mean nearly the same thing. Humans are good at the judgment calls that require context—knowing that in your specific research community, one name is preferred. By combining both, you get a fast, consistent consolidation without the blindness of pure automation or the cost of manual review.
798.po: The resulting clean ontology reduces duplicate properties and enforces naming consistency, making the knowledge graph more actionable for AI. Papers tested on a gold standard show that the consolidated schema is more concise (fewer redundant properties) and semantically clear, which improves the quality of AI systems that use the graph for reasoning.

799.bp: Scientists build on each other's work by citing prior papers, and getting cited is how the scientific community recognizes you. But citations aren't distributed fairly: some groups get cited more than their contribution warrants, while others are overlooked. This distorts which ideas survive, who gets funded, and whose voices matter in science.
799.wh: The key tension is distinguishing cause from correlation. Women do get fewer citations than men; people from elite institutions get more citations. But is it because their work is better? Because of bias? Because of who they know? The obvious answer (bias) turns out incomplete. Even if you equalize representation—put equal numbers of women and men in the field—disparities persist because of two subtler mechanisms: homophily (tendency to cite people similar to yourself, whether by gender or prestige) and preferential attachment (once you're cited more, you accumulate even more citations, a snowball effect).
799.ap: The authors build a model of how citation networks grow, incorporating three elements: homophily (you're more likely to cite your in-group), preferential attachment (high-citation authors get cited more), and group size (underrepresentation). They show that when you combine these three, the model reproduces the real disparities observed in the data. Then they can test: if we only change group size, does it fix the problem? Answer: no, not enough.
799.ww: This mechanism works because it reveals a feedback loop: if women cite women less (homophily) and early high-citation authors were mostly men (historical), then men accumulate a head start. That head start feeds on itself through preferential attachment—they're already cited, so they get cited more. Even when you add more women, they face the existing imbalance. It's a path-dependent system where early inequity locks in.
799.po: The concrete insight is that fixing scientific equity requires multiple levers: increasing representation (necessary but not sufficient), reducing homophily (broadening who you cite), making underrepresented groups more visible, and supporting newcomers to integrate fairly. The paper quantifies these effects, showing which interventions matter most. The broader payoff is a scientific web that's more transparent about its biases and evidence-based about what actually reduces them.

800.bp: When you query a knowledge graph (a database of interconnected facts), you often ask questions like 'is there a path from A to C?' or 'what can I reach from A?' These queries are fundamental to reasoning systems, recommendation, and security. But the straightforward answer—enumerate every path—can be inefficient or return meaningless results because of cycles and detours.
800.wh: There's a classic trade-off in graph theory: simple paths (paths without visiting the same node twice) are harder to compute—the problem is NP-complete, meaning no known fast algorithm works for all cases. In practice, systems cheat by allowing any path (including cycles), which is fast but returns bloated result sets full of detours that don't make semantic sense. The challenge is: can you get the best of both without paying the full cost?
800.ap: The paper proposes a clever indexing trick: instead of computing all simple paths on the fly, pre-compute a compact set of representative paths and store them in an index. The key is choosing which paths to pre-compute—the longest acyclic chains and the fundamental cycles that generate all others. At query time, you look up in the index and expand as needed, which is much faster than traversing the full graph. Because you've selected representative paths carefully, every result still conforms to simple path semantics (no repetition).
800.ww: This works because of a theorem from graph theory: you don't need all simple paths to answer connectivity queries correctly; a small basis of fundamental cycles and longest chains is sufficient. By identifying this basis and materializing it in an index, you trade pre-computation (done once) for query speed. It's the same principle that makes indices work for databases: spend time organizing data upfront so queries run fast later.
800.po: Experiments show that the index-based approach achieves near-perfect recall (finds the right answers) while outperforming prior systems by up to 10x on speed. It demonstrates that even for NP-complete problems, carefully designed approximations—'perfect approximations' that are empirically correct but computationally tractable—can be more valuable than waiting for an optimal solution that never arrives.

801.bp: As AI systems are deployed in the real world, we need the ability to remove or forget sensitive information—a person's data from a trained model after they ask to be deleted, a model trained on data that turns out to be mislabeled, or data that was maliciously inserted. Graph neural networks, which learn patterns across networks of connected data, make forgetting hard because removing one node or edge ripples through the entire learned model.
801.wh: The core difficulty is that neural networks don't store explicit facts; they learn compressed statistical patterns. Trying to remove a single data point means you need to somehow undo the model's learning from that point without retraining from scratch (which is expensive). With graphs, it's worse: one node touches many others, so the ripple effects are huge. Existing methods also lack a principled way to measure how well unlearning actually worked—did you really remove the information, or does it still leak through the learned patterns?
801.ap: The paper proposes MGU, which reframes unlearning through the lens of memorization: which data points did the model memorize (remember exactly), and which did it only partially absorb? The framework then targets high-memorization examples with strong unlearning and applies lighter touch to partially absorbed data. It also introduces practical difficulty assessment (no need to access test data) and a comprehensive evaluation protocol that checks whether the removed information actually leaks when you try to extract it.
801.ww: This works because memorization is a quantifiable property—you can estimate which examples a model memorized without exhaustive testing. By targeting unlearning to these high-memorization examples, you focus your effort where it matters. The framework also aligns the evaluation (testing what you actually care about—does the information leak?) with the goal (true forgetting), avoiding the mismatch in prior work that tested easy cases and missed hard ones.
801.po: MGU consistently outperforms prior unlearning methods across ten real-world graphs in three dimensions: better forgetting quality (the information is actually removed), faster computation (doesn't require retraining), and utility preservation (the model still works well on remaining data). This makes it practical for real-world systems where data must be deleted on demand.

802.bp: Live streaming platforms—Twitch, TikTok Live—need to recommend which stream to watch based on a user's interests, what's trending, and what interactions they've had. Unlike video platforms where content is static, live streams are dynamic: the topic changes, the audience changes, the engagement changes minute-by-minute. Recommender systems designed for static content fail at this volatility.
802.wh: The challenge is that most recommenders model users and content independently or assume content doesn't change much. But in live streaming, the 'room' (stream) is a dynamic entity that evolves constantly. Users interact in real-time within a room, creating signals about what the streamer is doing right now and what each user is interested in right now. Existing systems either ignore these fine-grained, real-time signals or model them too crudely to capture the room's evolution.
802.ap: DCGLive models the dynamic environment by tracking two things in parallel: the broader tripartite interactions (which users visit which rooms and who streams them) and the real-time collaboration within each room (what users are doing right now). It constructs dynamic bipartite graphs—snapshots of connections that change over time—and learns representations (numerical summaries) of rooms, streamers, and users that reflect these dynamics. Non-parametric collaboration indicators (statistics computed from interaction patterns) capture whether a room is heating up or cooling down.
802.ww: This works because decomposing the problem (broad trends plus local dynamics) lets you model both. The dynamic graphs capture how relationships shift; the collaboration indicators capture the real-time texture. By grounding recommendations in actual user interactions within a specific room, not generic user preferences, the system can adapt as the streamer pivots topics or the audience's interest changes.
802.po: DCGLive improves recommendation quality on live streaming platforms by accounting for the real-time evolution of streams and rooms. The concrete payoff is that users are recommended streams that match their current interests and momentum (rooms that are active and engaging right now), not just broad popularity or historical preferences.

803.bp: Many real-world networks are defined by when things happen, not just what happens: who contacted whom and when, which transactions occurred and in what order. Predicting the next connection or event in these temporal networks is crucial for forecasting communication, detecting fraud, and understanding information flow. But temporal graphs are harder to model than static ones because timing and sequence matter.
803.wh: The core problem is that existing temporal graph neural networks assume you memorize which specific neighbors connected to each node. But in sequential systems—millions of updates over time—each neighbor might appear only once or twice, so memorization fails. The networks are also sensitive to noise: when an unexpected event occurs (an unusual connection), the model overfits to it rather than generalizing to the underlying rhythm. Prior models struggle to capture the real structure when there's so much noise and so few repetitions.
803.ap: SeqFilter takes a different approach. Instead of memorizing neighbors, it focuses on when interactions happen (the rhythm of each node—when does this entity typically act?). It stores absolute timestamps with recency awareness, so recent events count more. Then, to model the local structure around a node, it uses frequency-selective filtering: amplifying or suppressing specific frequencies in the patterns of who connects to whom. This is like a radio dial that tunes into the right channel of a noisy broadcast.
803.ww: This works because it shifts the focus from 'who' to 'when.' In sequential systems, the rhythm of when someone acts is more informative than their identity (which is rare). Frequency-selective filtering lets the model learn what timescale matters: is the network driven by hourly patterns, daily patterns, or event-triggered bursts? By tuning to the right frequency, the model ignores noise at other frequencies.
803.po: SeqFilter achieves over 70% mean reciprocal rank (a measure of ranking quality) on temporal graph link prediction, a significant jump from prior methods that often failed below 70%. It's particularly effective on graphs with many sequential updates and sparse edge repetitions, which is the common case in real-world temporal networks.

804.bp: Predicting future values in a time series—tomorrow's stock price, next week's weather—requires capturing both the main trend (what a simple model would predict) and the complex residuals (the deviations from that trend that encode the hard-to-predict part). Modeling both well is the path to accurate forecasts, especially over long horizons.
804.wh: The tension is that most forecasting models excel at one or the other: they either predict the main trend well (but miss nuance) or they try to model everything and get lost in noise. Long-term forecasting is especially hard because errors accumulate and the future is far from the training examples. Generative diffusion models—which learn to generate complex distributions—have shown promise elsewhere but underperform on time series, probably because they don't specialize to the actual structure of time-series errors.
804.ap: Re-Diffusion separates the problem: first, use a traditional backbone predictor (any standard forecasting model) to get a rough prediction. Then, use a diffusion model to learn the distribution of residuals—the prediction errors. The key is that residuals are often simpler to model than the raw signal (they have less scale variation, more structure). The pipeline compresses residuals into a learned latent space, then uses conditional diffusion to generate likely residual distributions that reduce prediction bias.
804.wh: This works because diffusion models are good at capturing complex distributions, and residuals are more structured than raw signals. By targeting the model to the error rather than the raw forecasting problem, you align the tool to the job. Diffusion's strength—modeling intricate distributions—helps estimate not just the mean prediction but the full spread of possibilities. Combining a backbone predictor with residual diffusion gives you both the speed of traditional methods and the expressiveness of modern generative models.
804.po: Re-Diffusion achieves 10% improvement over state-of-the-art forecasters on long-term time-series prediction. It shows that generative models can enhance traditional forecasting by specializing to the residual structure rather than trying to model everything from scratch. The payoff is more accurate long-term predictions, which directly improves planning and decision-making.

805.bp: Graph neural networks learn patterns by aggregating information from connected neighbors. This works beautifully when neighbors tend to be similar (homophily: birds of a feather flock together). But in many real networks—academic collaboration graphs, biological networks—connections often link dissimilar nodes (heterophily). Standard graph networks break down in these cases because indiscriminately averaging dissimilar neighbors dilutes the signal.
805.wh: The problem has two parts. First, when you look at distant neighbors (two or three hops away), you often include more dissimilar nodes than similar ones, so aggregating them is harmful. Second, the local structure around each node varies: sometimes a few similar neighbors matter, sometimes distant structure matters, sometimes the pattern is complex. Prior solutions add more distant neighbors or reweight them, but they often amplify noise and miss these nuanced local variations.
805.ap: CSS-GCN combines two strategies. First, it partitions each node's local neighborhood (its ego-network) and applies fairness constraints to identify which structural patterns distinguish similar from dissimilar neighbors, learning domain-invariant structures. Second, it uses selective propagation: rather than blindly averaging all neighbors, it computes which neighbors are truly useful based on similarity, then gates (selectively routes) information through three pathways: similar neighbors, high-quality distant neighbors, and original features. This gating mechanism adapts the neighborhood aggregation to the local context.
805.ww: This works because selective propagation respects heterophily: it acknowledges that not all neighbors are equally useful and adapts aggregation to the local structure. The three pathways capture different intuitions (similar neighbors, distant but high-quality structure, intrinsic properties), and gating lets the model learn which combination is right for each node. By learning domain-invariant structural patterns first, you also reduce bias toward spurious structures.
805.po: CSS-GCN outperforms graph neural networks on heterophilic graphs where standard methods struggle. The payoff is that graph neural networks can now be applied reliably to networks like social graphs, academic collaboration, and biological systems where dissimilar nodes connect—a major expansion of where these methods work.

806.bp: Knowledge organizes itself hierarchically: there are broad categories, subcategories, specific items. When a new concept emerges—'deep learning for protein folding'—the knowledge system needs to figure out where to place it in the existing hierarchy by identifying its parent concepts (hypernyms: broader categories it belongs to). This taxonomy completion is essential for keeping knowledge graphs organized and usable as new research emerges.
806.wh: The core tension is that taxonomies have an imbalanced structure: there are many leaf nodes (specific items) but few non-leaf nodes (general categories). Most learning methods treat all edges equally, so they overfit to the common pattern (being a leaf) and underfit to rare patterns (being a parent category). This causes models to perform poorly on placement decisions for new concepts. Additionally, models often learn disconnected embeddings for similar concepts because they fail to exploit the hierarchical path structure.
806.ap: BLEND uses two parallel paths. One path fine-tunes a small language model optimized specifically for leaf classification (deciding which leaves a new concept should connect to), while another is fine-tuned for balanced classification (treating all edges equally). The model also applies contrastive learning on structure-encoded paths—forcing similar paths through the hierarchy to have similar learned representations. The combined loss function from both paths and the contrastive learning produces more robust hierarchical understanding.
806.ww: This works because it treats the imbalance explicitly: by training separate branches for the majority class (leaves) and the balanced view, neither dominates. Contrastive learning on paths ensures that structural similarity is captured in the learned space, so the model understands not just individual decisions but how concepts relate in the hierarchy. Lightweight fine-tuning of language models (rather than training from scratch) allows you to start with semantic understanding of concept names.
806.po: BLEND improves taxonomy completion recall (finding the right parent nodes) by up to 9.32% over prior methods while maintaining efficient inference. It demonstrates that tailored training strategies for imbalanced hierarchies can outperform generic approaches, with direct payoff for maintaining and extending large knowledge taxonomies.

807.bp: In marketplaces with a broker—a financial intermediary, a matchmaker, an auction house—the broker needs to decide what price to charge to make a deal happen between a buyer and seller. The broker wants to capture value (earn a fee) while still making the deal attractive to both parties. This is a fundamental problem in mechanism design: how to mediate transactions fairly and profitably.
807.wh: The core challenge is that you don't know true valuations upfront. You get one sample from each party's preference distribution, and you must decide now—there's no second chance to negotiate. Standard economic theory assumes you know distributions in full, so this is much harder. The presence of the broker adds a third player with their own profit motive, which can create misalignment: the broker might be tempted to overcharge and block deals that would have happened.
807.ap: The paper analyzes simple mechanisms that rely only on a single sample from each agent. For example: look at the buyer's valuation, the seller's valuation, and the broker's fee, then decide whether to make the deal and at what price. Under standard economic assumptions (monotone hazard rates, related to probability distributions), these simple mechanisms can achieve constant-factor approximations to three goals: gains-from-trade (how much value the transaction creates), social welfare (value to all parties), and broker profit.
807.ww: This works because constant-factor approximations are achievable with limited information. You don't need to know the full distribution; one sample plus knowledge of the distribution family (monotone hazard rates) is sufficient. The mechanism's simplicity—not trying to extract fine details—actually helps robustness: it can't be exploited by strategic behavior that relies on uncertainty.
807.po: The paper shows that the cost of having a broker is surprisingly small: the approximation factors degrade only slightly compared to bilateral trade without a broker. Practically, this means markets with intermediaries can still achieve near-optimal efficiency for participants, and the broker can be incentivized to facilitate rather than block deals. The result bridges theory (economic mechanisms) with practice (one-shot decisions with limited information).

808.bp: When you want to search across different domains—find similar images from database A using a query image from database B—you need to transfer learned patterns from a label-rich source domain to a label-scarce target domain. Hash-based retrieval (encoding images as short bit strings for fast comparison) is efficient, but domain shift breaks it: patterns learned on one domain don't transfer to another. Real-world labeling is also noisy, further hurting transfer.
808.wh: The dual challenge is that source domain labels are often noisy (crowdsourced, web-crawled), and domain shift is pronounced. Noisy labels confuse semantic alignment—the model learns wrong associations between domains. Most methods assume clean labels and address only domain shift. Additionally, hard target samples (those far from the source distribution) are difficult to label confidently, so methods that naively pseudo-label everything end up confusing the model.
808.ap: ELPA has two modules. Uncertainty-aware Noise Separation uses belief and uncertainty masses from an evidential learning model (which quantifies confidence in predictions) plus a Gaussian Mixture Model to distinguish clean examples from noisy ones, filtering training. Progressive Cross-domain Alignment uses a partial optimal transport mechanism that prioritizes pseudo-labeling for well-aligned target samples—those the model is confident about—and gradually expands to harder samples.
808.ww: This works because it addresses both problems in sequence. First, filter the noisy source domain to focus on reliable examples. Then, gradually shift the model to the target domain by starting with confident predictions (low-hanging fruit) and progressively including harder samples. Evidential learning and Gaussian Mixture models quantify uncertainty, so the system knows which examples to trust. This staged approach avoids the cascade of errors that occur when you naively label everything.
808.po: ELPA outperforms domain-adaptive hashing baselines across multiple benchmarks with various noise ratios. The concrete payoff is that you can now cross-domain retrieval (search via hashing) even when source labels are noisy and target labels are scarce—a practical requirement in real-world scenarios where labels come from imperfect sources.

809.bp: When an AI system encounters data that looks different from its training set—new kinds of inputs, edge cases, anomalies—it should flag them as out-of-distribution, not blindly make predictions. Out-of-distribution detection is essential for safe deployment: if a medical diagnostic system sees a rare symptom pattern, it should say 'I don't know' rather than guess. For graph data, this is especially hard because structure is complex.
809.wh: Graph data is tricky: a graph's properties come from its substructures (small motifs, communities, paths), not global statistics like average degree. Prior OOD detection methods built for regular data don't transfer well. Additionally, you rarely have labeled 'normal' and 'abnormal' graphs in practice—the problem is unsupervised. You must learn what in-distribution structure looks like without examples of out-of-distribution graphs.
809.ap: KEGOD uses two parallel branches to learn graph patterns: a graph neural network (which learns via message-passing on structure) and a graph kernel (an explicit mathematical function that measures structural similarity). By learning concordance—agreement—between these two different ways of measuring structure, the model captures structure implicitly (via neural networks) and explicitly (via kernels). It also includes a learnable augmentation generator to create alternative views of graphs while preserving key structures. A self-adaptive training mechanism tunes the relative sensitivity of each branch.
809.ww: This works because two branches forced to agree provide a consistency signal. If a graph looks in-distribution to the neural branch but out-of-distribution to the kernel branch (or vice versa), that inconsistency flags potential OOD samples. Augmentation ensures robustness by forcing the model to learn invariances. Kernels add explicit structural reasoning that neural networks alone might miss, providing complementary signals.
809.po: KEGOD reliably detects graphs that deviate from the training distribution in unsupervised settings. The payoff is safer graph-based systems: anomaly detection in networks, fraud flagging in transaction graphs, and identification of atypical structures in knowledge graphs—all without requiring labeled examples of anomalies.
